cards.title: Something's off
cards.body:
Sometimes an account gets **taken over**: someone else gets in, usually with a stolen or guessed password.

It happens to adults and big companies too. What matters is noticing quickly and knowing what to do, and by the end of this lesson, you will.

cards.title: Signs someone else got in
cards.body:
- Your password **suddenly doesn't work**.
- Emails about a **sign-in** or **password change** you didn't make.
- **Posts or messages** you didn't send, or friends asking about weird links from you.
- A **device you don't recognise** in the account's list of signed-in devices.
- **Sign-in codes** you didn't ask for.
- Your **recovery email or phone** has been changed. (That's the backup the account uses to reset your password.)

cards.prompt: A sign of a hack, or normal?

items.label: Alert: a sign-in you didn't make
Friends got links you didn't send
An unknown phone in your devices list
An email after you changed your password
A code while you were signing in

cards.explanation: Sign-ins, messages, password changes and devices that **weren't you** are signs of a hack. An email or code that arrives right after **you** did something is the account doing its job.
cards.hint: For each one, ask: did I do this, or did someone else?
cards.nudge: Alerts and codes are normal when they match something you just did. They're warning signs when they don't.

cards.title: What to do, step by step
cards.body:
1. **Tell a trusted adult.** You're not in trouble, and two heads are better than one.
2. **Change the password**, on a device you trust, in the real app or website. Make it new, strong and unique.
3. **Check the recovery email and phone** straight away, and remove anything that isn't yours. Otherwise the attacker could use them to reset your new password.
4. **Sign out of other devices**, from the account's security settings. That kicks out anyone else.
5. **Turn on [[two-step sign-in]]**, so a password alone can't get in again.

Then change that password anywhere else you used it, and warn friends if they got strange messages.

Can't get in at all? Use the app's official **"Forgot password"** or account recovery. **Never pay** someone who offers to get it back for you: that's a [[scam]].

cards.prompt: Put the first five steps in order.

items.label: Check the recovery email and phone

cards.explanation: **Tell a trusted adult**, **change the password**, **check the recovery email and phone** (so they can't reset it again), **sign out of other devices**, then **turn on two-step sign-in**.
cards.hint: Think about the reason for each step: getting help, a new lock, stopping them resetting it, kicking them out, then a second lock.
cards.nudge: Look back at the steps and the reason each one was given. Each step only works if the one before it is done.

cards.prompt: Your friends say you've been sending them strange links. You haven't.

steps.text: You can still sign in. What do you do first?

choices.text: Tell a trusted adult, and change your password
choices.consequence: Good start. The attacker's password no longer works.
You'd lose everything, and the attacker might already have your password for other sites.

choices.text: Ignore it. Friends will work it out
choices.consequence: Every hour gives the attacker more time to trick your friends.

steps.text: Your password is changed. What next?

choices.text: Check recovery details, sign out other devices, turn on two-step
choices.consequence: Whoever was in is kicked out and can't get back in. Then you warn your friends not to click.
The attacker may still be signed in on their device. Sign out other devices too.

cards.explanation: Tell an adult and change the password first. Then **check the recovery details**, **sign out other devices**, turn on **two-step sign-in**, and warn your friends.
cards.hint: Follow the steps from the lesson in order. Is changing the password enough on its own if someone is still signed in?

cards.prompt: Your account was taken over. Someone messages: **"I can get it back for you for $20."** What is this?

options.text: A scam: use the app's official account recovery

options.nudge: The lesson warned about people offering to recover accounts. Only the app's own recovery can do it.
Real support teams don't message you asking for money. Think about who offers this for a fee.

cards.explanation: Account "recovery services" in your messages are scams. Use the app's official **Forgot password** or account recovery, and never pay.
cards.hint: What did the lesson say about people who offer to get your account back?

cards.title: How accounts get taken
cards.body:
Most take-overs come from a few things you already know how to stop:

- a password **reused** from a site that had a [[data breach]]
- a password typed into a **fake website** from a [[phishing]] message
- a password that's **easy to guess**, or **shared** with a friend

A unique passphrase, two-step sign-in and a sharp eye for scams stop nearly all of them.

cards.prompt: You check your account's security settings.

steps.text: The **recovery email** is one you've never seen. What do you do?

choices.text: Remove it, add your own, and turn on two-step sign-in
choices.consequence: Now only you can reset the password.

choices.text: Leave it. It's only a backup
choices.consequence: The recovery email can reset your password, so whoever owns it could get back in.

cards.explanation: The **recovery email** can reset your password, so it must be yours. Remove anything you don't recognise, and add a second lock.
cards.hint: What is the recovery email used for?

cards.prompt: Your password was changed and you can't sign in at all. What's the best first move?

options.text: Use the app's official "Forgot password" or recovery

options.nudge: You'd lose everything in the old one, and the attacker keeps it. Try to get it back first.

options.text: Pay someone online to recover it
options.nudge: People offering paid recovery are scammers. Only the app's own recovery can help.

cards.explanation: The app's official recovery is the way back in. Tell a trusted adult, and never pay a stranger.
cards.hint: The lesson said what to use if you can't get in at all.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Signs: a password that stops working, **alerts you didn't cause**, messages you didn't send, unknown devices.
- Steps: **tell an adult**, **change the password**, **check recovery details**, **sign out other devices**, **turn on two-step sign-in**.
- Locked out? Use the **official recovery**. Never pay a "recovery" stranger.

Next: who to tell, and where to get help in Australia.
